3.title: Telling a story
3.html:
Stage 7 · Read

Read

A true story about a very bad morning.

The day everything went wrong

Last month I had a job interview in the city centre. I got up at six, had a quick breakfast and left home early.

First, the bus came late. I waited twenty minutes, and then I took a taxi. After that, I looked down and saw my shoes: one black, one brown!

In the end, I came forty minutes late. I met the manager at the door and said, “I'm so sorry!” She only laughed and gave me a cup of coffee. “It's OK,” she told me. “The office clock stopped this morning, so everyone was late today – me too!”

Two days later she called me. I got the job!

1The story is about…
Why

Everything went wrong — but in the end he got the job.

1He had an interview last month.
2The bus came on time.
3His shoes were two different colours.
4He came to the interview ten minutes late.
5He got the job.
Why

The bus came late. He was forty minutes late — but he got the job.

1The past of “leave” in the story is…
2The past of “see” is…
3The past of “give” is…
4Which word starts the first problem? “___, the bus came late.”
5Which words start the last part? “___, I came forty minutes late.”
Why

left · saw · gave. A story moves with First → Then → After that → In the end.

Notice

Before you read: the title is “The day everything went wrong.” What can go wrong before a job interview?

5.title: Famous people
5.html:
Stage 7 · Read

Read

Two global stars — and their languages.

Shakira

Shakira is a singer from Colombia. She is Colombian, but her grandparents are from Lebanon. Spanish is her first language, but she speaks four languages: Spanish, English, Portuguese and some Arabic. English is very important for her, because she is a big star in the USA, Spain and Brazil. Millions of people are fans of her songs.

Son Heung-min

Son Heung-min is a footballer from South Korea. He isn't Chinese or Japanese – he is Korean. His first big club was in Germany. He was only sixteen, so his German is very good. Later he was a star in London for ten years. His teammates are men from many different countries, so English is important for him too. His fans are people of all ages: men, women and children.

1Both texts are about…
Why

Countries, nationalities and languages — for a singer and a footballer.

1Shakira is Colombian.
2She speaks only Spanish.
3Her grandparents are from Lebanon.
4Son Heung-min is Chinese.
5His German is very good.
Why

She speaks Spanish, English, Portuguese and some Arabic. Son Heung-min is Korean.

1The plural of “person” in the text is…
2The plural of “country” is…
3“His teammates ___ men from many different countries.”
Why

people · countries · teammates are (plural).

Notice

Before you read: Shakira and Son Heung-min. What do you know about them?

6.title: The family tree
6.html:
Stage 8 · Read

Read

Read about a very famous family.

The royal family

Queen Elizabeth II was the queen of the United Kingdom for seventy years. Her husband was Prince Philip. Their oldest son is the king now – King Charles III.

Charles and his first wife, Diana, had two sons, William and Harry. Charles and Diana divorced in 1996. Today Charles's wife is Queen Camilla, so she is William's stepmother.

William is Charles's older son. His wife is Catherine. Their three children are George, Charlotte and Louis.

Harry is married to Meghan, and Harry and Meghan live in America now with their two children. Harry is George's uncle, so George is Harry's nephew, and Meghan is George's aunt. Harry's children are George's cousins.

1The text is about…
Why

It explains who is whose son, wife, brother, aunt in the royal family.

1Prince Philip was the Queen's husband.
2King Charles is the Queen's son.
3Catherine is Harry's wife.
4William and Catherine have three children.
5Meghan is George's aunt.
Why

Catherine is William's wife. Meghan — Harry's wife — is George's aunt.

1___ husband was Prince Philip. (the Queen)
2William is ___ older son. (Charles)
3Meghan is ___ aunt. (George)
Why

the Queen → Her. One person's → add 's: Charles's, George's.

Notice

Before you read: the title is “The royal family.” Do you know any people in the British royal family?

7.title: My perfect day
7.html:
Stage 8 · Read

Read

Three people describe the day they would live again.

My perfect day

Aruzhan, 29. “My perfect day is a quiet morning in town. I wake up at nine – no alarm! I get dressed and walk to a small café, and I have breakfast there. Then I read and relax. I never do the housework on my perfect day!”

Tom, 45. “I love my job, so my perfect day is a day at work. I get up at six, have a shower and leave home at seven. I usually take the bus. I always have a break at eleven. After work I do the shopping, and I go to bed early.”

Mei, 63. “My perfect day is with my grandson. He wakes up very early, so we watch the sunrise together. We often walk by the river after lunch. He goes to bed at eight, and then I relax.”

1Who loves their job?
2Whose perfect day is with another person?
Why

Tom says “I love my job”. Mei's perfect day is with her grandson.

1Aruzhan wakes up at nine.
2Aruzhan does the housework on her perfect day.
3Tom leaves home at six.
4Tom always has a break at eleven.
5Mei's grandson goes to bed at eight.
Why

Aruzhan never does the housework. Tom gets up at six but leaves home at seven.

1Mei writes: “He ___ up very early.” Which form is in the text?
2“He ___ to bed at eight.”
3Find the word in the text that means “the time when the sun comes up”.
Why

After he: wakes, goes. “We watch the sunrise together.”

Notice

Before you read: the title is “My perfect day.” Is your perfect day busy or quiet?

9.title: Jobs that make you happy
9.html:
Stage 7 · Read

Read

Two people who smile on Monday morning.

Jobs that make you happy

Do you smile on Monday morning? Nurses, mechanics, hairdressers, pilots – every job has good and bad days. But these two people love what they do.

Asel, 31. She's a photographer. She works freelance, from home, so she doesn't have a boss. “Do I earn a big salary? No, I don't,” she says. “But does a big office make you happy? It doesn't make me happy. I choose my hours.”

Marco, 44. He's a chef in a busy restaurant. He works full-time, and his hours are long. The kitchen is often stressful. So does he want a new job? No, he doesn't. “My colleagues are my second family,” he says. “We work, we laugh and we eat together. Does your job do that?”

Happy workers don't always earn a lot of money. They enjoy their work.

1Why are Asel and Marco happy at work?
Why

Happy workers don't always earn the most — they enjoy their work.

1Asel works freelance, from home.
2Asel has a boss.
3Marco works short hours.
4The kitchen is often stressful.
5Happy workers always earn the most money.
Why

Asel doesn't have a boss. Marco works long hours. Happy workers don't always earn the most.

1Asel asks: “Does a big office ___ you happy?”
2“She's ___ photographer.”
3Find the word that means “people you work with”.
Why

Does + base verb: make · a photographer · colleagues = people you work with.

Notice

Before you read: the title is “Jobs that make you happy.” What makes a job good — money, people, or free time?

13.title: My perfect neighbourhood
13.html:
Stage 7 · Read

Read

What does a perfect neighbourhood need — and where is the strangest one?

My perfect neighbourhood

What does a perfect neighbourhood need? A website asked two thousand people. A park is at the top of the list. Number two is a supermarket, and number three is a chemist. There are always cafés and a library on the list too. A cinema is number six, but a swimming pool is only number nine. There isn't an airport on the list – airports are very noisy! People want a quiet, safe area with some trees.

And a very strange neighbourhood? Neft Dashlari is a town on an oil platform in the Caspian Sea. There are streets, houses and a hospital. There's a school, but there isn't a university. And there aren't any tourists – only workers live there.

1The text is about…
Why

First the perfect neighbourhood — then the strangest one.

1A park is at the top of the list.
2A swimming pool is more important than a cinema.
3Neft Dashlari is a town on an oil platform.
4There are a lot of tourists in Neft Dashlari.
5There's a school there, but there isn't a university.
Why

The cinema wins(!). Neft Dashlari: a school yes, a university no — and no tourists.

1“There ___ always cafés and a library.”
2“There ___ any tourists.”
3Find the word that means “an area of a town where people live”.
Why

cafés (plural) → are · tourists → aren't any · neighbourhood.

Notice

Before you read: what is number one for you — a park, a café or a supermarket?

14.title: Flats from the internet
14.html:
Stage 7 · Read

Read

The flat in the photo — and the flat in real life.

The ad

FOR RENT: a bright studio flat in the city centre of New York. It's on the fourth floor of a quiet building, with a big window and a view of the city. The flat is cosy and modern, with a new fridge, a sofa and a shelf for your books. The neighbours are friendly. The rent is only $800 a month!

The real flat

I live in the flat from the ad. The photo was beautiful. The flat is… small. Very small. There is only one room: the kitchen, the sofa and the table are all in it. There isn't a cupboard. My bed is on a shelf above the kitchen. The building is opposite a garage, so the street is noisy at night. But the rent is $800, the view is great – and I don't want to move!

1What is the big difference between the ad and the reality?
Why

The photo was beautiful — the flat is small. Very small.

1The ad says the flat is in the city centre.
2The flat has three rooms.
3The bed is on a shelf above the kitchen.
4The street is quiet at night.
5She wants to move.
Why

One room only · the garage makes the street noisy · but she loves it — “I'm not moving!”

1“FOR RENT: ___ bright studio flat” — why a?
2“___ flat is… small.” (text 2)
3Find the word that means “the money you pay every month for a flat”.
Why

first mention → a · now we know which → the · rent.

Notice

Before you read: $800 a month in New York. Good price or bad price? Guess!

16.title: How-to videos
16.html:
Stage 7 · Read

Read

Three 30-second how-to videos.

Read each script — and play it out loud.

Video 1 — the battery

Phone battery dying? First, open Settings. Then turn on dark mode. The dark screen uses less power. Next, close your old apps. Don't watch videos! Finally, turn down the brightness.

Video 2 — the tea

Perfect tea in four steps. First, boil fresh water. Don't use old water from the kettle. Then warm the cup. Next, put the tea in and wait four minutes. Don't press the tea bag! Finally, add a little milk.

Video 3 — the bag

A heavy bag? Make it light. First, take everything out. Then make two groups: every day, and maybe one day. Put the maybe things on a shelf. Don't carry five pens. One pen is enough! Finally, enjoy your light bag.

Video 1 — the batteryRead aloud by your device
Video 2 — the teaRead aloud by your device
Video 3 — the bagRead aloud by your device
1All three videos…
Why

Three little problems, three step-by-step answers.

1Dark mode uses less power.
2For perfect tea, use old water from the kettle.
3You wait four minutes for the tea.
4The bag video says: carry five pens.
Why

Dark mode saves power · boil fresh water · four minutes · one pen is enough!

1Find a negative instruction from video 2:
2“Make it ___” — the opposite of heavy.
3Which word starts the LAST step in every video?
Why

Don't + base verb · heavy ↔ light · the last step starts with Finally.

Notice

Before you read: 30 seconds is very short. How many steps can fit — three, five or ten?

17.title: What you could and couldn't do
17.html:
Stage 7 · Read

Read

Shopping and travel — thirty years ago and today.

Thirty years ago

Thirty years ago you couldn't buy everything in one shop. You bought bread at the baker's, meat at the butcher's and a newspaper at the newsagent's. You couldn't pay with your phone – it was cash or a cheque. You couldn't compare prices at home. You could book a holiday only at a travel agent's, and the maps in cars were on paper. But shop assistants knew their customers, and people had time for a chat.

Today

Today you can do almost everything online. You can compare prices in a minute, and you can pay with your phone. You can order dinner in one minute. You can buy a coffee from a vending machine at midnight. It's easy – but the internet can't cut your hair, and a machine can't have a friendly chat with you. That is still impossible.

1The texts say…
Why

You can do almost everything online — but a machine can't cut your hair or chat.

1Thirty years ago you could pay with your phone.
2You could book a holiday only at a travel agent's.
3The maps in cars were made of paper.
4Today the internet can cut your hair.
5People in the shops had time for a chat.
Why

Cash or cheque only · paper maps · and no, the internet still can't cut your hair.

1“You ___ compare prices at home.” (text 1)
2“You ___ order dinner in one minute.” (text 2)
3Find the word that means “a friendly talk”.
Why

then → couldn't · now → can · a friendly talk = a chat.

Notice

Before you read: what do you think was BETTER thirty years ago?

18.title: Instagram stories
18.html:
Stage 7 · Read

Read

Three people, three stories, one Saturday.

One Saturday

@aizhan_kz · 10 a.m. It's raining outside, but I'm in my favourite café. I'm not drinking coffee today – I'm drinking hot chocolate. I'm wearing my new yellow jumper and my old jeans, and my coat and scarf are on the chair. I'm very comfortable and warm!

@marat.runs · 8 a.m. Twenty minutes before my first marathon! I'm not running yet – I'm standing with three thousand people. I'm wearing a T-shirt, gloves and my lucky trainers. The sun is shining. I couldn't sleep last night, and now my heart is going boom-boom. I'm a little nervous!

@tila_travel · 6 p.m. This photo is from the Great Wall this morning. Right now I'm lying on my hotel bed. My boots are on the floor, and my feet hurt! My friends are having dinner downstairs, but I'm staying here.

1Who is very comfortable and warm?
2Who is a little nervous?
Why

Aizhan is in a café with hot chocolate; Marat's heart is doing boom-boom before the marathon.

1Aizhan is drinking coffee.
2It's raining where Aizhan is.
3Marat is running right now.
4Tila is standing on the Great Wall right now.
5Tila's feet hurt.
Why

Hot chocolate, not coffee · Marat is not running yet · Tila is lying on the bed NOW — the Wall photo is from earlier today.

1“I'm ___ on my hotel bed.” (lie)
2“The sun ___ shining.”
3What is Aizhan wearing?
Why

lie → lying · the sun is shining · a new yellow jumper.

Notice

Before you read: when do people usually post stories — on a boring day or a special day?

22.title: Where your food comes from
22.html:
Stage 8 · Read

Read

A recipe — and the numbers behind the rice.

Plov for six people

Ingredients: half a kilo of beef, a kilo of rice, four carrots, two onions, a little oil and some salt.

Chop the onions and the carrots. Heat the oil and fry the beef. Add the vegetables and a little salt. Then add the rice and some water. Don't add too much water, and don't add it quickly – add a little at a time. Cook for forty minutes. Add a few raisins at the end, mix, and serve!

How much food do countries grow?

Papua New Guinea grows about three-quarters of its food. Singapore is very different: it grows less than 10 per cent. There isn't enough land in a city-state, so it imports a lot of food. Indonesia grows a lot of rice, and forty million people work on farms – one sixth of all Indonesians. But Indonesians eat a lot of rice, and the country still imports about three million tonnes a year.

1The two texts are about…
Why

First the recipe, then the food numbers of three countries.

1You need half a kilo of beef.
2You must add a lot of water quickly.
3Singapore grows most of its food.
4Papua New Guinea grows about three-quarters of its food.
5Indonesia imports rice.
Why

Don't add too much water! Singapore grows less than 10%. Indonesia imports ~3 million tonnes.

1“Add ___ raisins at the end.”
2“There isn't ___ land in a city-state.”
3“One sixth of all Indonesians” — how do you write it?
Why

raisins → a few · not enough land · one sixth = 1/6.

Notice

Before you read: plov for six people — how much rice do you think you need?

25.title: A changing climate
25.html:
Stage 7 · Read

Read

The weather here — thirty years ago and today.

Read the two texts. Then listen to the short story of the same idea.

The 1990s

In the 1990s, the winters here were long and freezing. The snow came in November and stayed until April. Minus thirty was normal, and the river was icy for five months. Children played on it. The ice was thicker than a wall. The summers were short, and they were often wet and windy. The storms weren't very strong, and the air in the cities was clean.

Today

Today the winters are warmer and shorter than in the 1990s. The snow often comes in December and leaves in February. The summers are hotter and drier, and the storms are stronger than before. The forecast for July often says “boiling”. There is more pollution in the cities, too. The winters aren't as long as they were. The climate is changing faster than the old people can believe.

The same story, out loudRead aloud by your device
1The texts say…
Why

Warmer winters, hotter and drier summers, stronger storms.

1In the 1990s the snow came in November.
2Minus thirty was unusual then.
3Today the snow often leaves in February.
4The storms are weaker now.
Why

Minus thirty was normal · the storms are stronger now.

1“The ice was ___ than a wall.”
2“The climate is changing ___ than the old people can believe.”
3Find the word that means “dirty air in cities”.
Why

thicker · faster · pollution.

Notice

Before you read: ask someone older — were the winters really colder before?

26.title: World records
26.html:
Stage 7 · Read

Read

The highest, the deepest, the oldest — and one big surprise.

World records

Everest is the highest mountain on Earth, but Kilimanjaro is the highest mountain in Africa. It is one of the easiest big mountains to climb, and it is very popular. The oldest person to climb it was 89.

Lake Baikal in Russia is the deepest and the oldest lake in the world. It is 1,642 metres deep, and it has almost 20 per cent of the world's fresh water. Greenland is the biggest island, and the Pacific is the biggest and the deepest ocean.

And the biggest desert? Most people say the Sahara, but Antarctica is bigger than the Sahara. A desert is a very dry place, not a hot place. Antarctica is the coldest and the driest place on Earth – so it is the biggest desert, too.

The busiest airports are in big cities with a large population.

1What is the surprising record?
Why

Antarctica — the coldest AND driest place — is technically the biggest desert.

1Kilimanjaro is the highest mountain on Earth.
2Baikal has almost 20% of the world's fresh water.
3The Sahara is the biggest desert.
4The oldest person to climb Kilimanjaro was 89.
Why

Kilimanjaro is the highest in Africa (Everest on Earth) · Antarctica beats the Sahara · and yes — 89 years old!

1“It is ___ the easiest big mountains to climb.”
2“The ___ airports are in big cities.”
3Find the word that means “the number of people”.
Why

one of the easiest + plural · busiest · population.

Notice

Before you read: which is the biggest desert in the world? Are you sure?

28.title: A rule book for tourists
28.html:
Stage 7 · Read

Read

A rule book for visitors to Japan.

A rule book for visitors to Japan

Before your flight, check your passport. You have to carry it with you in Japan. You don't have to speak Japanese – a lot of signs are in English, and people are very polite.

In homes and in some restaurants, you have to take off your shoes. It's an old custom. You shouldn't eat while you walk in the street – people think it's rude. You shouldn't talk loudly on the train or on the underground, either.

Trains are almost never late: a delay of five minutes is big news! Big luggage on a busy train? You should send it to your hotel. You have to carry some cash, because a lot of small shops don't take cards. And you don't have to give tips. Tips aren't a custom in Japan.

1The text is…
Why

What you have to do, should do — and don't have to do.

1You have to speak Japanese.
2You have to take off your shoes in homes.
3You should eat while you walk in the street.
4You have to carry some cash.
5You have to give tips.
Why

Japanese is optional · shoes off — yes · no eating while walking · cash — yes · tips — don't have to!

1“You don't have to give tips” means…
2“You shouldn't talk loudly on the train” is…
3Find the word that means “a tradition, a normal way of doing things”.
Why

don't have to = optional · shouldn't = advice · custom.

Notice

Before you read: what do you know about the rules in Japan? Shoes? Tips? Trains?
